Writing for Small Screens: How to Structure Text for E-Readers

by Daily Writing Tips
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:49
Instaread

You finish a chapter on your laptop and it looks perfect. Then you open the same file on a six-inch e-reader, bump the font up two sizes, and your tidy paragraph becomes a gray wall that fills three screens.

To structure text for e-readers, you have to plan for that moment. Keep paragraphs short, use real headings, keep lists simple, and remove anything that depends on a fixed page. This guide shows you how to do each one, with examples you can apply to your next manuscript.

Why Does Text Behave Differently on an E-Reader?

E-reader text behaves differently because it reflows. The words rearrange themselves to fit the screen, the font, and the size the reader chooses.

Understanding Reflowable Text

Most ebooks use reflowable text. The W3C’s EPUB 3 overview describes EPUB as a format built for content that adapts to different screens and reading settings, rather than one that locks every line in place.

That flexibility shifts control from you to the reader. You can’t decide where a line breaks or where a “page” ends. You can only decide how the text is organized.

What This Means for Your Writing

On paper, a long paragraph looks like one solid block. On a phone-sized screen at a large font, the same paragraph may stretch across several screens with no visual break.

Structure is the only layout that survives reflow. If your ideas are broken into clear units, the reader can follow them on any device.

How Long Should Paragraphs Be for E-Readers?

Paragraphs for e-readers should be shorter than they would be in print. Aim for one idea per paragraph and two to four sentences in most cases.

Following the One-Idea Rule

The Purdue OWL’s guide to paragraphs gives the classic rule: each paragraph develops one idea, and a new idea gets a new paragraph. On a small screen, that rule matters even more, because each break gives the reader a place to rest.

Plain-language guidance points the same way. The Digital.gov guide to short sentences and paragraphs recommends paragraphs of no more than 150 words and notes that long blocks can discourage readers from continuing.

Examples: Splitting a Dense Paragraph

  • Weak: The new policy takes effect in March, and every team will need to update its forms, which means managers should schedule training in February, although teams that already use the digital forms can skip the first session and go straight to the review meeting.
  • Why it fails: Four ideas share one sentence. On a narrow screen, the reader loses the thread before the end.
  • Strong: The new policy takes effect in March. Every team will need to update its forms. (New paragraph) Managers should schedule training in February. Teams that already use the digital forms can skip the first session.
  • Why it works: Each paragraph carries one point, and the break signals a shift from what is changing to what managers should do.

Shortening Sentences Too

Long sentences cause the same problem as long paragraphs. Front-load the subject and verb so the reader knows who does what before the line wraps.

The active voice helps here, since active sentences are usually shorter and more direct than passive ones.

How Should You Use Headings in an Ebook?

Use headings often, keep them short, and apply them as true heading styles, not as bold body text. Headings are how readers find their place on a device with no visible page numbers.

Applying Real Heading Styles

When you format a heading with your word processor’s Heading 1 or Heading 2 style, conversion tools recognize it as a heading. That allows the ebook to build a working table of contents and helps screen readers announce the structure.

Bold text at a larger size looks like a heading to you but often converts as an ordinary paragraph. The reader then loses navigation for that section.

Keeping Headings Short and Specific

A heading that runs three lines in print may run five on a phone. Keep headings to a few words and make them describe what follows.

  • Weak: Some Additional Thoughts on the Various Considerations Involved
  • Why it fails: It’s long, vague, and tells the reader nothing about the section.
  • Strong: Choosing a File Format
  • Why it works: The reader knows the topic at a glance, even on a small screen.

Checking Heading Alignment

Amazon’s Kindle text guidelines for reflowable books note that reflowable body text is fully justified by default, so they recommend setting an explicit alignment for headings. Without it, a short heading can stretch with uneven gaps between words.

How Do You Format Lists, Tables, and Notes for Small Screens?

Format them as simply as possible. Short vertical lists work well, wide tables rarely do, and footnotes need a different approach entirely.

Keeping Lists Short and Parallel

Bulleted lists are easy to scan on a small screen, but only if each item is brief and built the same way. Start every item with the same part of speech, and keep nesting to one level.

The Chicago Manual of Style’s Q&A on vertical lists covers how to punctuate and capitalize list items. Whatever style you choose, apply it the same way throughout the book.

  • Weak list items: Saving drafts often / You should back up files / Version names
  • Strong list items: Save drafts often / Back up your files / Name each version clearly

Replacing Wide Tables

A table with five columns may fit a printed page but force sideways scrolling on an e-reader, or shrink to an unreadable size. Ask whether the content truly needs a grid.

  • Two-column tables: Usually display well. Keep them.
  • Wide comparison tables: Convert each row into a short subsection or a bold-label list.
  • Data tables that must stay intact: Consider an image with a full text description nearby.

Handling Footnotes and Page References

E-readers don’t have fixed pages, so phrases such as “see page 42” or “as shown on the facing page” stop making sense. Replace them with section names or internal links: “see Choosing a File Format.”

Footnotes usually convert into linked notes that open in a pop-up or jump to the end of a chapter. Keep notes short, and move anything essential into the main text so readers don’t have to tap away to understand it.

How Do You Prepare and Test Your File?

Prepare your file from a clean, well-styled manuscript, then test it on more than one screen size before you publish.

Starting From the Right Source

A word processor file with consistent styles converts more cleanly than a print-ready PDF, because a PDF locks every line in place. If your manuscript only exists as a print layout, a pdf to epub converter can give you a reflowable file to work from, but you’ll still need to check every heading, list, and paragraph break by hand.

Separating Paragraphs Correctly

Amazon’s guidelines require body paragraphs to be distinguished with either a first-line indent or extra space between paragraphs. Pick one method and use your paragraph style settings to apply it, never the Tab key or the space bar.

Testing Like a Reader

Before you publish, open the file and read it the way your audience will:

  1. Change the font size: Try the smallest and largest settings.
  2. Switch orientation: Read a chapter in portrait and landscape.
  3. Use the table of contents: Tap every entry to confirm it lands in the right place.
  4. Follow every link: Check internal cross-references and notes.
  5. Read one chapter start to finish: Watch for paragraphs that feel too long on screen.

What Are the Most Common Structure Mistakes in Ebooks?

The most common mistakes come from writing for a printed page that the reader will never see. Watch for these five:

  1. Page-number references: “See page 12” points to nothing on a device.
  2. Fake headings: Bold body text that never shows up in the table of contents.
  3. Overlong paragraphs: Print-length blocks that fill several screens.
  4. Spacing with the keyboard: Tabs, extra spaces, or blank lines used for layout often disappear or behave unpredictably after conversion.
  5. Passive, wordy sentences: Long constructions are harder to follow when lines wrap often. These examples of passive voice and how to fix them show how to tighten them.

How Can You Summarize Writing for Small Screens?

Writing for e-readers means building structure into the words themselves. Keep paragraphs to one idea, keep sentences direct, and use real heading styles so readers can navigate.

Simplify lists and tables, replace page references with section names, and test your file at several sizes before release. For more practical guides on clear, correct writing, subscribe to the Daily Writing Tips newsletter.
